claim: CCKBR(A) expression is approximately 100-fold higher in FSH cells than in LH cells in tilapia
source: In tilapia, the expression of this receptor is ~100- fold higher in FSH than in LH cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome data from sorted pituitary cells shown in Figure 1A

claim: LH cells express the CCK receptor (CCKBR(A)) at a lower level than FSH cells
source: Nevertheless, LH cells also express the CCK receptor (CCKBR(A)) albeit at a lower level (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The CCKBR(A) receptor is predominantly expressed in FSH cells in zebrafish
source: We, therefore, first validated its expression on gonadotroph cells in zebrafish using in situ hybridization and found that the receptor is predominantly expressed in FSH cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B

claim: CCK-secreting neuronal projections innervate the pituitary near FSH cells and adjacent to GnRH axons
source: We found hypophysiotropic CCK-secreting neuronal projections innervating the pituitary near FSH cells and adjacent to GnRH axons (Figure 1C), indicating hypothalamic input of CCK into the pituitary gland.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1C

claim: All homozygous CCKBR(A) mutant fish were males with significantly small gonads
source: Analysis of the phenotype of F2 adult fish (5–6 mo of age) revealed that while non-edited (wt/wt, n=15) and heterozygous fish (CCKBR(A)wt/+12, CCKBRBwt/+7, CCKBR(A)wt/-1, n=20) displayed typical sex ratios and functional adult gonads, all homozygous fish (CCKBR(A)+12/+12, CCKBR(A) +7/+7,CCKBR(A)-1/-1, n=12) were males with significantly small gonads (Figure 1D–E; mean gonad area KO = 3.8 ± 0.48 mm^2, Heterozygous = 23.52 ± 10.6, WT = 78 ± 7.4 mm^2).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis and measurements shown in Figure 1D-E

claim: The testes of CCKBR(A) mutant males displayed an immature phenotype with mostly early stages of testicular germ cells
source: The testes of mutant males displayed an immature phenotype as they were populated mostly by early stages of testicular germ cells (mostly spermatogonia and spermatocytes) and contained low volumes of mature spermatozoa compared to their WT and heterozygous siblings (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1F

claim: CCKBR(A) loss-of-function mutants show decreased expression levels of both lhβ and fshβ genes
source: Indeed, our mutants show decreased expression levels of both lhβ and fshβ genes (Figure 1G), suggesting that loss of CCK signaling affects both LH and FSH.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 1G

claim: The phenotype of CCKBR(A) LOF fish closely resembles zebrafish with loss-of-function mutations in both gonadotropin genes
source: Instead, the phenotype of the CCKBR(A) LOF closely resembles the condition reported for zebrafish that have LOF mutations in both gonadotropin genes (Zhang et al., 2015b; Chu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by comparison to published literature on gonadotropin mutants

claim: In fish, LH and FSH are secreted by distinct cell types in the pituitary
source: In fish, LH and FSH are secreted by distinct cell types in the pituitary.
evidence: Established fact about fish pituitary biology

claim: FSH signaling controls folliculogenesis in fish
source: In recent years, different loss-of-function (LOF) studies revealed the stereotyped function of each gonadotropin: FSH signaling controls folliculogenesis, whereas the role of LH is restricted to the induction of ovulation (Takahashi et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015a; Chu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited loss-of-function studies

claim: The role of LH is restricted to the induction of ovulation in fish
source: In recent years, different loss-of-function (LOF) studies revealed the stereotyped function of each gonadotropin: FSH signaling controls folliculogenesis, whereas the role of LH is restricted to the induction of ovulation (Takahashi et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015a; Chu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited loss-of-function studies

claim: Adult zebrafish with loss-of-function of GnRH signaling are fertile
source: For a yet unknown reason, in the zebrafish, even a complete absence of GnRH does not impair ovulation, as adult zebrafish with LOF of GnRH signaling are fertile (Tanaka et al., 2022; Spicer et al., 2016; Whitlock et al., 2019), suggesting that GnRH activity is either replaced by a compensation mechanism or it is dispensable for the control of gonadotropin release overall.
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies on GnRH loss-of-function zebrafish

claim: In medaka, the effects of GnRH are limited to the control of final oocyte maturation and ovulation via LH secretion
source: In other species, such as medaka, the effects of GnRH are limited to the control of final oocyte maturation and ovulation via LH secretion (Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited study on medaka

claim: In the basal state, LH cells were mostly silent
source: In the basal state, LH cells were mostly silent, whereas FSH cells exhibited short (mean of 10.08 s half width) calcium bursts (mean of 0.6 ΔF/F; Figure 2C (fish1) and Figure 2D; Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: Supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C and 2D

claim: FSH cells exhibited short calcium bursts with a mean half width of 10.08 seconds and mean amplitude of 0.6 ΔF/F in the basal state
source: In the basal state, LH cells were mostly silent, whereas FSH cells exhibited short (mean of 10.08 s half width) calcium bursts (mean of 0.6 ΔF/F; Figure 2C (fish1) and Figure 2D; Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: Supported by in vivo calcium imaging measurements shown in Figure 2D

claim: In seven out of ten zebrafish, LH cells exhibited a single long and strong calcium rise
source: In seven out of ten zebrafish, we observed an event in which LH cells exhibited a single long (mean of 75.55 s half-width) and strong (mean of 1.5 ΔF/F) calcium rise (Figure 2C (fish2) and D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C and 2D

claim: The calcium rise in LH cells was synchronized between LH cells with a mean max cross-correlation coefficient of 0.89 ± 0.003
source: This event was synchronized between LH cells (mean max cross-correlation coefficient values of 0.89 ± 0.003) and, in three out of seven fish, it was followed by a less synchronized (mean max cross-correlation coefficient values, 0.66 ± 0.011,) calcium rise in FSH cells (Figure 2C (fish2) and Figure 2D, Figure 2—video 3).
evidence: Supported by cross-correlation analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C and 2D

claim: The max cross-correlation coefficient values of all active LH cells were significantly higher compared to FSH cells
source: On average, the max cross-correlation coefficient values of all active LH cells were significantly higher compared to FSH cells (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which reflects the strong gap-junction mediated coupling between LH cells that does not exist in FSH cells (Golan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of cross-correlation data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Strong gap-junction mediated coupling exists between LH cells but does not exist in FSH cells
source: On average, the max cross-correlation coefficient values of all active LH cells were significantly higher compared to FSH cells (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which reflects the strong gap-junction mediated coupling between LH cells that does not exist in FSH cells (Golan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited previous study and inferred from correlation data

claim: GnRH application elicited a response in 95% of LH cells
source: Overall, whereas GnRH elicited a response in 95% of LH cells, only 56% of FSH cells responded to the treatment in the same fish (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Only 56% of FSH cells responded to GnRH treatment
source: Overall, whereas GnRH elicited a response in 95% of LH cells, only 56% of FSH cells responded to the treatment in the same fish (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E

claim: GnRH induced a strong and slow calcium rise in LH cells with average half width of 48.6 seconds and average amplitude of 1.99 ΔF/F
source: In response to GnRH puff application (300 μl of 30 μg/μl, 78.74 µM), LH cells exhibited a strong and slow calcium rise (average half width 48.6 s and average amplitude of 1.99 ∆F/F; Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Figure 3—video 1 (GnRH) and 3), which was synchronized between the cells, as observed by the increase in correlation values from 0.26 ± 0.02–0.66 ± 0.05 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo calcium imaging measurements shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: CCK elicited a strong calcium response in FSH cells with 40.3–172 second half-width and mean amplitude of 1.44 ΔF/F
source: CCK elicited a strong calcium response (40.3–172- s half-width, mean amplitude of 1.44 ∆F/F) in FSH cells, while in some of the fish, a lower response was observed in LH cells (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo calcium imaging measurements shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: In all analyzed fish, all FSH cells responded to CCK
source: In all analyzed fish (n=7), all FSH cells responded to CCK, whereas the number of LH cells that responded to the stimulation varied widely (20–100%, n=7; Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The calcium response in FSH cells to CCK was highly synchronized with mean max cross-correlation coefficient of 0.7 ± 0.04
source: The calcium response in FSH cells was highly synchronized (mean max cross-correlation coefficient, 0.7 ± 0.04; Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: The response of LH cells to CCK application was characterized by low mean of max cross-correlation coefficient values of 0.43 ± 0.05
source: By contrast, the response of LH cells to CCK application was characterized by low mean of max cross-correlation coefficient values (0.43 ± 0.05; Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: GnRH stimulation resulted in a significant rise in LH secretion
source: As expected, the calcium response to GnRH in LH cells was followed by a significant rise in LH secretion (n=5; Figure 5A, LH concentration ranging from 0.1 to 2 ng/ml).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 5A

claim: FSH cells responded with a very low rise in hormonal secretion in response to GnRH treatment that was not significant from basal secretion
source: In contrast, FSH cells responded with a very low rise in hormonal secretion in response to GnRH treatment (FSH concentration ranging from 0.003 to 0.06 ng/ml) that was not significant from the basal secretion.
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 5A

claim: CCK application elicited a significant calcium rise in FSH cells followed by an elevation of FSH concentration in the medium
source: Conversely, the application of CCK elicited a significant calcium rise in FSH cells followed by an elevation of FSH concentration in the medium (FSH concentration ranging from 0.5 to 5 ng/ml), whereas in LH cells, no significant effect was observed on calcium activity, and the slight increase in LH secretion was not significant (n=5; LH concentration ranging from 0.25 to 0.75 ng/ml Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging and ELISA measurements shown in Figure 5B

claim: CCK injection significantly increased the expression and secretion of FSH in vivo
source: These results were reproduced in vivo, as CCK injection significantly increased the expression and secretion of FSH (Figure 5C and D) whereas the response to GnRH did not reach statistical significance (p=0.069).
evidence: Supported by in vivo injection experiments shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: GnRH only affected LH expression in the pituitary
source: GnRH only affected LH expression in the pituitary (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Three types of CCK receptors (CCKAR, CCKBR, and CCKBR(A)) are reported in the genome of fish
source: While three types of CCK receptors (CCKRs; CCKAR, CCKBR, and CCKBR(A)) are reported in the genome of fish, only one type (CCKBR(A), XM_017357750.2) is expressed in the pituitary gland (Hollander-Cohen et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by cited previous study and expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: Only CCKBR(A) is expressed in the pituitary gland
source: While three types of CCK receptors (CCKRs; CCKAR, CCKBR, and CCKBR(A)) are reported in the genome of fish, only one type (CCKBR(A), XM_017357750.2) is expressed in the pituitary gland (Hollander-Cohen et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by cited previous study and expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: CCK expression in the brain is directly connected to the metabolic status of the fish
source: CCK expression in the brain is directly connected to the metabolic status of the fish, as starved fish have a significant decrease in CCKB expression compared to fed fish (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by starvation experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: Starved fish have a significant decrease in CCKB expression compared to fed fish
source: CCK expression in the brain is directly connected to the metabolic status of the fish, as starved fish have a significant decrease in CCKB expression compared to fed fish (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data from starvation experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: The 12 bp insertion added four amino acids that disrupted the structure of the CCKR transmembrane domain of the receptor
source: The three identified mutations induced by gRNA number two. The 7 bp insertion and 1 bp depletion created a frameshift that disrupted the translation of the RNA, while the 12 bp insertion added four amino acids that disrupted the structure of the CCKR transmembrane domain of the receptor.
evidence: Supported by mutation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The CCK ligand stimulated WT CCKR but not the mutated receptors in a COS-7 reporter assay
source: The CCK ligand stimulated WT CCKR but not the mutated receptors in a COS-7 reporter assay.
evidence: Supported by receptor transactivation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: Heterozygous fish displayed significantly lower amounts of spermatozoa compared to WT fish
source: Heterozygous fish were also affected and displayed significantly lower amounts of spermatozoa compared to the WT fish.
evidence: Inferred from histological analysis mentioned in the text

claim: CCKBR(A) is highly expressed in the pituitary and in the hypothalamus
source: Tissue distribution of the CCK receptors reveals the high expression of CCKBR(A) in the pituitary and in the hypothalamus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), which are both central areas of the HPG axis.
evidence: Supported by tissue distribution data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: In mammals, both LH and FSH are secreted by the same cell population
source: While in mammals, both LH and FSH are secreted by the same cell population, in fish these gonadotropins are produced by discrete cell types (Hollander-Cohen et al., 2021; Golan et al., 2016).
evidence: Established knowledge about mammalian pituitary biology

claim: In fish, gonadotropins are produced by discrete cell types
source: While in mammals, both LH and FSH are secreted by the same cell population, in fish these gonadotropins are produced by discrete cell types (Hollander-Cohen et al., 2021; Golan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited previous studies

claim: Most FSH calcium transients were not associated with a rise in calcium in LH cells
source: Since most FSH calcium transients were not associated with a rise in calcium in LH cells, we speculated that a cell type-specific regulatory mechanism drives the activity of the two cell types and GnRH and CCK are the primary candidates.
evidence: Inferred from calcium imaging observations

claim: A cell type-specific regulatory mechanism drives the activity of LH and FSH cells
source: Since most FSH calcium transients were not associated with a rise in calcium in LH cells, we speculated that a cell type-specific regulatory mechanism drives the activity of the two cell types and GnRH and CCK are the primary candidates.
evidence: Speculated based on observed differences in calcium activity patterns

claim: GnRH and CCK are the primary candidates for cell type-specific regulation of gonadotrophs
source: Since most FSH calcium transients were not associated with a rise in calcium in LH cells, we speculated that a cell type-specific regulatory mechanism drives the activity of the two cell types and GnRH and CCK are the primary candidates.
evidence: Speculated based on observed activity patterns and receptor expression

claim: In 50% of fish, FSH cells displayed an increase in cross-correlation values in response to GnRH
source: In contrast, in FSH cells only 50% of the fish displayed an increase in cross-correlation values from the basal state (Figure 3D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: The number of LH cells that responded to CCK stimulation varied widely from 20–100%
source: In all analyzed fish (n=7), all FSH cells responded to CCK, whereas the number of LH cells that responded to the stimulation varied widely (20–100%, n=7; Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C

claim: CCK preferentially activates FSH cells in fish
source: These results indicate that in fish, CCK preferentially activates calcium rise in FSH cells, albeit with a weaker activation of LH cells.
evidence: Concluded from calcium imaging and secretion data

claim: GnRH preferentially controls LH secretion in zebrafish
source: Here, we reveal that in zebrafish, CCK, a satiety hormone, gates reproduction by directly regulating GtH secretion. We show that GnRH preferentially controls LH secretion and identify CCK as the long-sought hypothalamic FSH secretagogue.
evidence: Concluded from calcium imaging and hormone secretion experiments

claim: CCK is the hypothalamic FSH secretagogue in zebrafish
source: Here, we reveal that in zebrafish, CCK, a satiety hormone, gates reproduction by directly regulating GtH secretion. We show that GnRH preferentially controls LH secretion and identify CCK as the long-sought hypothalamic FSH secretagogue.
evidence: Concluded from calcium imaging, hormone secretion, and loss-of-function experiments

claim: CCK gates reproduction in zebrafish by directly regulating gonadotropin secretion
source: Here, we reveal that in zebrafish, CCK, a satiety hormone, gates reproduction by directly regulating GtH secretion.
evidence: Concluded from multiple lines of evidence including loss-of-function, calcium imaging, and hormone secretion data

claim: The disruption of GnRH and its receptors didn't lead to any drastic effect on reproduction in zebrafish
source: Interestingly, in contrast to GnRH, the novel CCK regulation identified under the current study has a more substantial effect on the gonadotrophic axis, as revealed in our mutants, while the disruption of GnRH and its receptors didn't lead to any drastic effect on reproduction (Tanaka et al., 2022; Spicer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited studies on GnRH loss-of-function

claim: CCK regulation has a more substantial effect on the gonadotrophic axis than GnRH in zebrafish
source: Interestingly, in contrast to GnRH, the novel CCK regulation identified under the current study has a more substantial effect on the gonadotrophic axis, as revealed in our mutants, while the disruption of GnRH and its receptors didn't lead to any drastic effect on reproduction (Tanaka et al., 2022; Spicer et al., 2016).
evidence: Concluded by comparing phenotypes of CCK receptor mutants to published GnRH mutants

claim: CCK is a satiety hormone in multiple species of mammals and fish
source: The role of CCK as a satiety hormone has been demonstrated in multiple species of mammals and fish (Lõhmus et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2017; Lo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies

claim: In oviparous species, folliculogenesis constitutes the main nutritional challenge during the female reproductive cycle
source: In oviparous species, the pre-ovulatory processes of gonadal development involving vitellogenin synthesis and deposition into the developing oocyte, also known as folliculogenesis, constitute the main nutritional challenge during the female reproductive cycle.
evidence: Based on knowledge of oviparous reproductive biology

claim: In oviparous species, folliculogenesis is gated by the animal's nutritional status
source: Thus, in oviparous species, folliculogenesis is gated by the animal's nutritional status.
evidence: Inferred from the energetic demands of folliculogenesis

claim: Dedicated hypothalamic neurons have developed to integrate metabolic cues to induce reproduction in fish
source: Our data suggest that, indeed, dedicated hypothalamic neurons have developed to integrate metabolic cues, such as food abundance and somatic condition, to induce the energetically costly process of reproduction in fish.
evidence: Concluded from the CCK-mediated regulation of FSH and its connection to satiety

claim: CCK is a regulator of satiety in fish
source: Since CCK is a regulator of satiety in fish (Himick and Peter, 1994; Zhang et al., 2017; Volkoff, 2006), this hypothalamic circuit directly links the metabolic status of the fish to its reproductive capacity (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies

claim: The hypothalamic CCK circuit directly links the metabolic status of the fish to its reproductive capacity
source: Since CCK is a regulator of satiety in fish (Himick and Peter, 1994; Zhang et al., 2017; Volkoff, 2006), this hypothalamic circuit directly links the metabolic status of the fish to its reproductive capacity (Figure 6).
evidence: Concluded from the role of CCK in both satiety and FSH regulation

claim: CCK has an FSH-regulating role in medaka
source: Considering the recent report of an FSH-regulating role for CCK in the distantly related species medaka (Uehara et al., 2023), our findings represent a highly conserved mechanism for controlling reproduction in fish.
evidence: Supported by cited recent study in medaka

claim: The CCK-mediated control of reproduction represents a highly conserved mechanism in fish
source: Considering the recent report of an FSH-regulating role for CCK in the distantly related species medaka (Uehara et al., 2023), our findings represent a highly conserved mechanism for controlling reproduction in fish.
evidence: Inferred from findings in both zebrafish and medaka

claim: The lack of females in CCKBR(A) LOF mutants suggests a direct disruption of both LH and FSH circuitry
source: The lack of females in our LOF mutant, together with the male's infertility, suggests a direct disruption of both LH and FSH circuitry.
evidence: Inferred from the phenotype of the mutants

claim: CCK directly controls FSH cells by innervating the pituitary gland and binding to specific receptors
source: We further show that CCK directly controls FSH cells by innervating the pituitary gland and binding to specific receptors that are particularly abundant in FSH gonadotrophs.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry, receptor expression, and functional data

claim: CCK activates LH cells either directly or indirectly by affecting LH cells via activation of GnRH or other neurons
source: This activation may either be direct, as LH cells were also shown to express the CCK receptor (Hollander-Cohen et al., 2021) albeit at a lower level, or indirectly, by affecting LH cells via activation of GnRH or other neurons.
evidence: Speculated based on receptor expression and anatomical observations

claim: GnRH3 and CCK terminals are in close apposition in the zebrafish pituitary
source: The latter pathway can be wired through the close apposition of GnRH3 and CCK terminals in the zebrafish pituitary, as shown in this work.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1C

claim: In mammals, GnRH neurons express CCK receptors
source: Additional support is the evidence in mammals where GnRH neurons express CCK receptors and CCK directly affects the migratory pathway of GnRH during development (Giacobini et al., 2004; Giacobini and Wray, 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited studies in mammals

claim: CCK directly affects the migratory pathway of GnRH during development in mammals
source: Additional support is the evidence in mammals where GnRH neurons express CCK receptors and CCK directly affects the migratory pathway of GnRH during development (Giacobini et al., 2004; Giacobini and Wray, 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited studies in mammals

claim: CCK-producing axons innervate the zebrafish pituitary
source: Our identification of CCK-producing axons innervating the zebrafish pituitary suggests a predominantly central CCK-dependent control of FSH release.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data

claim: In fish, hypothalamic neurons directly innervate the pituitary and secrete their regulatory peptide close to the destination cells
source: While in mammals, hypothalamic regulation of the pituitary is gated by the median eminence, in fish, hypothalamic neurons directly innervate the pituitary and secrete their regulatory peptide close to the destination cells (Golan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited previous study

claim: Similar CCK innervation of the pituitary was observed in lamprey
source: Similar innervation of CCK was observed in ancient jawless fish, such as lamprey (Sobrido-Cameán et al., 2020), and modern teleosts, such as the goldfish (Himick and Peter, 1994).
evidence: Supported by cited studies in lamprey and goldfish

claim: Modern oviparous tetrapods express the CCK receptor in their pituitary glands
source: Modern oviparous tetrapods were also shown to express the CCK receptor in their pituitary glands (Wan et al., 2023), indicating that this regulatory circuit may be evolutionarily conserved and common to oviparous vertebrates.
evidence: Supported by cited study in oviparous tetrapods

claim: The CCK regulatory circuit may be evolutionarily conserved and common to oviparous vertebrates
source: Modern oviparous tetrapods were also shown to express the CCK receptor in their pituitary glands (Wan et al., 2023), indicating that this regulatory circuit may be evolutionarily conserved and common to oviparous vertebrates.
evidence: Inferred from CCK receptor expression across diverse oviparous species

claim: CCK increases concomitantly in the gut and in the brain in response to feeding
source: Nevertheless, the direct innervation of CCK terminals into the pituitary gland and the concomitant increase of CCK in the gut and in the brain in response to feeding (Zhang et al., 2017; Gomes et al., 2022; D'Agostino et al., 2016) suggest that the two sources of CCK are interconnected.
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies

claim: The vagal nerve may serve as a gut-brain communication route for CCK satiety signals
source: In this context, the vagal nerve may serve as a possible gut-brain communication route, as it was shown to relay satiety signals to the hypothalamus via CCK (Borgmann et al., 2021; Clemmensen et al., 2017), thus forming a parasympathetic regulatory loop onto the hypothalamo-pituitary-gonadal axis.
evidence: Speculated based on cited studies showing vagal relay of CCK signals

claim: CCK loss-of-function mice can reproduce
source: Unlike the situation in fish, CCK LOF mice can reproduce (Lo et al., 2010), reflecting that the main metabolic challenge in the reproductive cycle of mammals is controlled by placental gonadotropins rather than by the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.
evidence: Supported by cited study in mice

claim: The main metabolic challenge in the reproductive cycle of mammals is controlled by placental gonadotropins rather than by the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
source: Unlike the situation in fish, CCK LOF mice can reproduce (Lo et al., 2010), reflecting that the main metabolic challenge in the reproductive cycle of mammals is controlled by placental gonadotropins rather than by the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in CCK LOF phenotypes between fish and mammals

claim: FSH cells express a different type of GnRH receptor than LH cells
source: However, since FSH cells express a different type of GnRH receptor (Hollander-Cohen et al., 2021), their activation is less consistent and results in reduced gonadotropin secretion.
evidence: Supported by cited previous study

claim: LH and FSH are co-secreted during the female spawning cycle in zebrafish
source: Importantly, similar functional overlap also exists in the potency of GnRH to activate FSH cells, corresponding to a previous finding where LH and FSH are co-secreted during the female spawning cycle (So et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by cited previous study

claim: Functional overlap in gonadotropin signaling pathways exists in the gonad through the promiscuity of the two gonadotropin receptors
source: Moreover, in the zebrafish, as well as in other species, the functional overlap in gonadotropin signaling pathways is not limited to the pituitary but is also present in the gonad, through the promiscuity of the two gonadotropin receptors (So et al., 2005; Hollander-Cohen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by cited studies

claim: Multilevel overlap in gonadotropin signaling creates functional redundancy that grants the reproductive system a high level of robustness
source: This multilevel overlap creates functional redundancy that grants the reproductive system a high level of robustness and ensures the species' persistence.
evidence: Inferred from the observed functional overlaps at multiple levels

claim: Metabolically driven hypothalamic circuits evolved to control gonad development in fish
source: Overall, our findings propose an updated view of the regulation of gonadal function in fish, in which metabolically driven hypothalamic circuits evolved to control gonad development.
evidence: Concluded from the CCK-mediated regulation of FSH and its connection to metabolic status

claim: Aquaculture has become the dominant supplier of fish for human consumption
source: In addition to the novel insight into the evolution and function of the reproductive axis in oviparous animals, these findings are also of particular importance in the context of aquaculture, which has become the dominant supplier of fish for human consumption in the face of declining yields from wild fisheries (Froehlich et al., 2018; Anderson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited studies on aquaculture

claim: The CCK circuit is the main gateway between metabolic state and reproduction in fish
source: With the identification of the CCK circuit as a regulator of folliculogenesis and the main gateway between metabolic state and reproduction, novel tools targeting this pathway can now be designed to manipulate gonadal development and overcome challenges in gamete production and the control of puberty onset in farmed fish (Zohar, 1989; Taranger et al., 2010).
evidence: Concluded from the demonstrated role of CCK in regulating FSH and its connection to metabolic status

claim: Novel tools targeting the CCK pathway can be designed to manipulate gonadal development in farmed fish
source: With the identification of the CCK circuit as a regulator of folliculogenesis and the main gateway between metabolic state and reproduction, novel tools targeting this pathway can now be designed to manipulate gonadal development and overcome challenges in gamete production and the control of puberty onset in farmed fish (Zohar, 1989; Taranger et al., 2010).
evidence: Speculated application based on the findings

claim: The secretion of both gonadotropins by gonadotrophs is controlled by the hypothalamic neuropeptide GnRH according to existing dogma
source: According to the existing dogma, the secretion of both GtHs by gonadotrophs of the anterior pituitary gland is controlled by the hypothalamic neuropeptide GnRH, which is produced by a small population of neurons in the preoptic area (Belchetz et al., 1978).
evidence: Supported by cited study establishing the dogma

claim: Differential control over gonadotropin secretion in mammals is attained via changes in frequencies and amplitude of GnRH pulses
source: Studies conducted in mammals have shown that the differential control over gonadotropin secretion is attained via changes in frequencies and amplitude of GnRH pulses (Savoy-Moore and Swartz, 1987; Stamatiades and Kaiser, 2018; Thompson and Kaiser, 2014), as well as by a variety of other endocrine and paracrine factors that dictate whether the cells will secrete LH or FSH.
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies in mammals

claim: In fish, activin, inhibin, follistatin, and PACAP signalling exert a differential effect on FSH and LH synthesis
source: In fish, the TGF-β family members activin, inhibin, and follistatin, as well as PACAP signalling have been shown to exert a differential effect on FSH and LH synthesis (Yuen and Ge, 2004; Aroua et al., 2012; Yaron et al., 2001; Lin and Ge, 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies in fish

claim: The hypothalamic mechanisms governing the differential release of FSH or LH in non-mammalian vertebrates remain largely unknown
source: However, the hypothalamic mechanisms governing the differential release of FSH or LH in non-mammalian vertebrates remain largely unknown.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field

claim: Other hypothalamic neuropeptides can bypass GnRH and directly regulate gonadotropin secretion in fish
source: However, in recent years, its status as the sole neuropeptide regulating GtH secretion has been called into question, as other hypothalamic neuropeptides were shown to bypass GnRH and directly regulate gonadotropin secretion (Biran et al., 2008; Tsutsui et al., 2012; Biran et al., 2014a; Biran et al., 2014b; Ogawa et al., 2016; Cohen et al., 2020; Mitchell et al., 2020; Rajeswari and Unniappan, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies

claim: Fish brains express up to three forms of GnRH due to genome duplication events
source: Due to genome duplication events, fish brains express up to three forms of GnRH, of which one form (usually GnRH1) innervates the pituitary gland (Tello et al., 2008; Okubo and Nagahama, 2008).
evidence: Supported by cited studies on fish GnRH evolution

claim: In zebrafish, the gene encoding GnRH1 has been lost, and GnRH3 has become the dominant hypophysiotropic form
source: In some species, such as the zebrafish, that express only two forms of GnRH (GnRH2 and GnRH3), the gene encoding GnRH1 has been lost, and GnRH3 has become the dominant hypophysiotropic form (Okubo and Nagahama, 2008).
evidence: Supported by cited study on zebrafish GnRH

claim: The loss of GnRH in zebrafish and medaka does not affect gonadal development
source: Since in both species the loss of GnRH does not affect gonadal development, the hypothalamic factor controlling FSH secretion in fish remains unknown (Takahashi et al., 2016; Spicer et al., 2016; Marvel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies on GnRH loss-of-function

claim: The hypothalamic factor controlling FSH secretion in fish was unknown prior to this study
source: Since in both species the loss of GnRH does not affect gonadal development, the hypothalamic factor controlling FSH secretion in fish remains unknown (Takahashi et al., 2016; Spicer et al., 2016; Marvel et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap that this study addresses

claim: CCK is produced in the fish hypothalamus
source: Using in vivo and ex vivo calcium imaging in zebrafish gonadotrophs to identify LH- and FSH-specific secretagogues, we show that the two types of gonadotrophs vary significantly in their activity patterns and that GnRH controls LH cells whereas FSH cells are preferentially activated by the satiety hormone CCK, which is also produced in the fish hypothalamus (Himick and Peter, 1994; Sobrido-Cameán et al., 2020) and its receptor is highly expressed in FSH cells (Hollander-Cohen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by cited studies

claim: The two types of gonadotrophs vary significantly in their activity patterns
source: Using in vivo and ex vivo calcium imaging in zebrafish gonadotrophs to identify LH- and FSH-specific secretagogues, we show that the two types of gonadotrophs vary significantly in their activity patterns and that GnRH controls LH cells whereas FSH cells are preferentially activated by the satiety hormone CCK, which is also produced in the fish hypothalamus (Himick and Peter, 1994; Sobrido-Cameán et al., 2020) and its receptor is highly expressed in FSH cells (Hollander-Cohen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data

claim: Mutating the CCK receptor results in a severe hindrance to ovarian development
source: We found that FSH cells express a CCK receptor, and our findings demonstrate that mutating this receptor results in a severe hindrance to ovarian development.
evidence: Supported by phenotypic analysis of CCKBR(A) mutants

claim: Mutating the CCK receptor causes a complete shutdown of both gonadotropins secretion
source: Additionally, it causes a complete shutdown of both gonadotropins secretion.
evidence: Supported by gene expression and hormone secretion data from mutants

claim: GnRH predominantly activates LH cells
source: Using in-vivo and ex-vivo calcium imaging of gonadotrophs, we show that GnRH predominantly activates LH cells, whereas FSH cells respond to CCK stimulation, designating CCK as the bona fide FSH secretagogue.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments

claim: FSH cells respond to CCK stimulation
source: Using in-vivo and ex-vivo calcium imaging of gonadotrophs, we show that GnRH predominantly activates LH cells, whereas FSH cells respond to CCK stimulation, designating CCK as the bona fide FSH secretagogue.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging experiments

claim: The control of gametogenesis in fish was placed under different neural circuits that are gated by CCK
source: These findings indicate that the control of gametogenesis in fish was placed under different neural circuits, that are gated by CCK.
evidence: Concluded from the differential regulation of LH and FSH by GnRH and CCK

claim: The insertion of a four-amino acid sequence at the start of TM4 of the CCKBR(A) receptor led to receptor inactivation
source: However, this insertion of a four-amino acid sequence (Asp-Asp-Ser-His) at the start of TM4 of the CCKBR(A) receptor, specifically between amino acids 188 and 192, led to receptor inactivation.
evidence: Supported by receptor transactivation assay data

claim: Amino acid 192 is part of the binding site for the mammalian CCKR2
source: A study by Foucaud et al., 2008 demonstrated that amino acid 192 is part of the binding site for the mammalian CCKR2.
evidence: Supported by cited study

claim: Modifications in the region around amino acid 192 significantly impact the CCKR receptor's ligand-binding characteristics and overall functionality
source: Our findings indicate that modifications in this region, significantly impact the receptor's ligand-binding characteristics and overall functionality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by receptor transactivation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E
